analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prices for the most expensive brand-name drugs and caps what seniors pay out of pocket.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 230-192 in December 2019, but the Senate never brought it to a vote and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate maximum prices for insulin and for dozens of the costliest brand-name drugs with no generic competition, capping those prices at roughly what other wealthy countries pay [S3]. It would have required drugmakers to pay rebates when their prices rise faster than inflation, added a hard cap on seniors' yearly out-of-pocket drug costs, and expanded Medicare to cover dental, vision, and hearing care [S3]. The House passed it 230-192, but it sat on the Senate calendar and never received a vote before the Congress ended [S6].
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and people with high drug costs gain the most: negotiated prices for selected drugs must be offered through Medicare, and private plans can take them too [S3]. Seniors on Medicare Part D get a lower out-of-pocket threshold with no cost-sharing above it, and Medicare gains coverage for dental, vision, and hearing care [S3]. Low-income beneficiaries get expanded subsidy eligibility [S3]. Community health centers, NIH, FDA, and opioid-response programs receive new funding [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and people with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to negotiate maximum prices for insulin and at least 25 (rising to 50) high-cost brand-name drugs with no generic competition; under current law HHS is prohibited from negotiating drug prices.
Caps the negotiated maximum price at no more than 120% of the average price in Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom — far below typical U.S. prices.
Applies negotiated prices to Medicare and allows private health plans to use them, so savings can reach people with employer or individual coverage, not just Medicare.
Requires manufacturers to pay rebates to Medicare when prices of drugs costing $100 or more rise faster than inflation.
Lowers the Medicare Part D out-of-pocket threshold, eliminates cost-sharing above it, and expands Medicare to cover dental, vision, and hearing services.
Expands low-income subsidies, bans abusive spread pricing by pharmacy benefit managers in Medicaid, and funds community health centers and opioid-response programs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear the cost: negotiated maximum prices below current U.S. prices, an excise tax on sales that escalates to 95% for manufacturers that refuse to negotiate, civil penalties, and inflation rebates [S3][S4]. Pharmacy benefit managers lose the spread-pricing practice in Medicaid [S3]. Insurers that participate pay less for selected drugs; taxpayers may absorb some shifted revenue through program funding, and patients could see slower development of some new drugs if manufacturer revenue falls.

drawbacks.text: Tying U.S. prices to the lowest foreign prices could cut manufacturer revenues and, as opponents argued, slow the development of new medicines; an amendment offered on the floor would have delayed the bill until HHS certified it would not reduce new drug applications for unmet medical needs.

The negotiation program reaches only a set of the most expensive single-source drugs, and private insurers can opt out of the negotiated prices, so savings would not automatically reach everyone with commercial coverage.
The escalating excise tax on manufacturers that do not comply — up to 95% of sales — is a blunt enforcement tool that critics said functions as effective price control rather than negotiation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: lower prices on the costliest drugs, a real out-of-pocket cap for seniors, and dental, vision, and hearing coverage for Medicare. The main honest cost is the risk that sharply lower revenue on selected drugs modestly reduces incentives to develop new medicines, though the bill protects drugs once generics or biosimilars exist and funds NIH and FDA innovation programs with part of the savings [S3][S4]. The program's narrow scope and the private-insurer opt-out limit how far savings reach [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 230-192, but the Senate let it sit on its calendar without ever voting, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Introduced in September 2019, the bill was referred to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — and each reported it amended in December 2019.
On December 12, 2019, the House rejected a Republican motion to recommit that would have delayed the bill until HHS certified it would not reduce new drug applications, by a vote of 196-226.
The House then passed the bill 230-192, with 228 of 228 voting Democrats in favor, 2 Republicans in favor, and 191 Republicans opposed.

The Senate received the bill on December 16, 2019, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on September 8, 2020; no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: prices stayed unregulated, Medicare still cannot negotiate, and the out-of-pocket and dental-vision-hearing benefits never took effect. Senate leadership that declined to schedule a vote preserved the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug manufacturers and Senate leadership

for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and steered it through committee markup and House floor passage.

for.name: Richard Neal
for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: His committee marked up and reported the bill, including the Medicare negotiation and rebate provisions in its jurisdiction.

for.name: House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously to pass the bill on December 12, 2019.

for.name: Nancy Pelosi
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the House floor under a rule allowing structured debate and amendments.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate vote; it sat on the Senate calendar from December 2019 until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republicans

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost perfectly by party: 228 of 228 voting Democrats voted yes, while 191 of 193 voting Republicans voted no, with 2 Republicans in favor [S7].

industries.note: The bill forces maximum prices capped near foreign levels, rebates for inflation-busting price hikes, and an excise tax of up to 95% of sales for manufacturers that refuse to negotiate [S3][S4]. The industry's revenue depends on charging U.S. prices far above what other countries pay, which is exactly what the bill targets.

The bill bans spread pricing and requires pass-through pricing in Medicaid, ending a practice where intermediaries keep the difference between what they charge the state and what they pay pharmacies [S3].
Private plans may obtain selected drugs at the negotiated maximum price, lowering their costs, but they can opt out and the program does not mandate their participation [S3].
Adding dental, eyeglass, and hearing-aid coverage to Medicare would make millions of seniors paying customers for care they currently go without [S3].
